name: The Species-Area Relationship
statement: The larger the area you look at, the more species you find.
meaning: The species-area relationship is the observation that the number of species found in a habitat rises with the area sampled — larger areas hold more species. It is most often modelled as a power law, species number equal to a constant times area raised to an exponent, so that on a log-log plot species and area fall on a straight line whose slope is that exponent. It is one of the oldest and most general patterns in ecology.
mechanism: Several forces contribute, and which dominates is debated. Larger areas simply contain more individuals, and more individuals sample more species. They also encompass more habitat types, each with its own species. On true islands, larger area means lower extinction and so more species at equilibrium. And there is a purely statistical accumulation, as rarer species turn up the more area, and the more individuals, one examines. The exponent tends to be higher for isolated islands, around a fifth to a third, and lower for nested mainland samples.

examples.text: Olof Arrhenius fitted species number as a power of area in 1921, the form still most used, giving a straight line of slope equal to the exponent on log-log axes.
Gleason proposed a semi-log form in 1922, arguing the power law predicts impossibly many species for very large areas; real data often fall between the two curves.
Running the relationship backward, shrinking area to forecast species lost to habitat destruction, is a common but contested use, which He and Hubbell argued always overestimates extinction.

variants.name: Island versus nested curves
variants.text: The island relationship across discrete isolates, typically steeper, versus the nested mainland relationship within contiguous plots, typically shallower and triphasic — distinct constructions often conflated.

variants.name: Preston's canonical form
variants.text: Frank Preston's 1962 link to the lognormal distribution of species abundances, which yields a theoretical exponent near a quarter and fed into island biogeography theory.

whyItMatters: It is ecology's closest thing to a law, a pattern so general it underlies estimates of biodiversity, forecasts of extinction from habitat loss, the design of nature reserves, and the theory of island biogeography. Its very ubiquity makes getting its form and its exponent right consequential for how we count species and predict their loss.

working.text: estimate how many species an area holds by fitting the power law, reading the exponent from the log-log slope.
distinguish island, nested, and accumulation curves, which have different slopes and should not be conflated.
use the backward relationship to predict species loss only with care, since it can badly misestimate extinction.

limits: The exponent varies widely with taxon, spatial scale, and whether the data are islands or mainland; it is no universal constant. The functional form is unsettled, power law competing with semi-log and hybrid models, and real points often lie between them. The relationship is scale-dependent, the nested curve steep at small scales, flatter at intermediate ones, and steep again at continental scales. And using it to predict extinctions is genuinely contested: He and Hubbell argued the backward relationship always overestimates species loss, since the area needed to remove a species' last individual far exceeds that needed to encounter its first — though others argue it can underestimate instead.
misreadings: The species-area relationship is not a single law or curve; island, nested, and accumulation curves are distinct constructions with different slopes, and conflating them is a documented error. The exponent is not a fixed constant near a quarter; that is a theoretical value, while empirical exponents range widely and depend on scale and system. And you cannot simply reverse the curve to predict extinctions, a step that biases the estimate in ways still debated.
origin: One of ecology's oldest patterns, given the power-law form by Olof Arrhenius in 1921 and a semi-log form by H. A. Gleason in 1922, and linked to species abundance by Frank Preston in 1962; its use in forecasting extinction was challenged by He and Hubbell in 2011.

sources.text: He & Hubbell, "Species-area relationships always overestimate extinction rates from habitat loss," Nature 473:368-371 (2011). — the argument against reversing the curve to predict extinction.
Matthews et al., "Island species-area relationships and species accumulation curves are not equivalent," Global Ecology and Biogeography 25 (2016). — the distinction between the curve types.
Tjorve, "The species-area relationship, self-similarity, and the true meaning of the z-value," Ecology (2008). — the exponent's variation and interpretation.
